continuity_scope: A character-layer pass for the Bhagavad Gītā as the 18-chapter Sanskrit dialogue embedded in the Mahābhārata's Bhīṣma Parva. It treats the Gītā as a sacred textual unit, not as a stand-alone fantasy setting or a substitute for the wider epic. Verse numbering follows the 700-verse received Gītā as presented by IIT Kanpur's Gita Supersite; the embedded location is cross-checked against scholarly reference to the Poona/BORI edition.

work_or_witnesses.edition: Sanskrit root verses, with selectable translations and commentaries, Gita Supersite, Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur
Oxford Bibliographies in Hinduism entry by Simon Brodbeck; contextual reference only

coverage_rule: Include every named speaker or framing interlocutor who materially performs the bounded dialogue: the opening questioner, the reporting narrator, and the two direct interlocutors. A name merely catalogued in the battlefield scene, named only in an analogy, or displayed on a banner is excluded unless that figure speaks or materially acts within this textual unit. This rule yields Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Sañjaya, Arjuna, and Kṛṣṇa.
omissions: Battlefield names in chapter 1 that do not become speaking or materially acting agents within this bounded dialogue, including Duryodhana, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the named warriors in the army catalogue.
Vyāsa, though named in Sañjaya's closing statement, because he does not speak or materially act in the bounded dialogue; no cross-source character endpoint is created for him.
Hanumān on Arjuna's banner, divine beings named in illustrative or revelatory speech, unnamed armies, places, chariots, and concepts.
The wider Mahābhārata narrative, Harivaṃśa, regional recensions, translations, commentarial schools, devotional retellings, performances, and modern adaptations.
Claims about contemporary Hindu practice, universal Hindu doctrine, or consensus among traditions beyond the cited verse and explicitly identified commentary layers.
uncertainties: The Gītā has extensive and sometimes divergent commentarial, philosophical, linguistic, devotional, and reception histories. This pass records root-text claims and identifies commentary only as commentary, not as a settled universal reading.
The Gita Supersite is a scholarly/institutional digital presentation, not a new critical edition. Verse locators should be checked against a chosen printed critical edition for source-critical work.

The precise relation of the received 700-verse Gītā to Mahābhārata manuscript and critical-edition layers requires specialist textual-critical review; Oxford identifies it as Mahābhārata 6.23–6.40 in the Poona edition.
Dharma, yoga, karma, bhakti, prakṛti, guṇa, ātman, and divya cakṣus are retained as source-language terms. They are not equivalences for alignment, class, spell, resource, race, or game mechanic.
evidence_basis: Claim-specific Sanskrit-verse locators use IIT Kanpur's Gita Supersite, which presents the root text alongside clearly labeled translation/commentary layers. Oxford Academic supports the embedded-text context and received chapter/verse framing. The four-person boundary is intentionally narrower than SRC-277's 49-character Mahābhārata BORI companion pass. The same names are independently represented with SRC-278 IDs; no identity merge or claim transfer to SRC-277 is implied.

citations.locator: Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā, root-text book view; opening verse 1.1
supports: Declared Sanskrit dialogue witness and its framed opening speakers.
The Gītā is an embedded part of the Sanskrit Mahābhārata; it is chapters 6.23–6.40 in the Poona edition and has 18 chapters/700 verses.
